Q: How do trace context, sampling and data redaction change what operators can conclude?
A:
Trace context connects related spans across asynchronous and remote boundaries; missing propagation can split one operation into unrelated observations. Sampling decides which traces are retained and can bias visible failures or latency.

Redaction must apply before sensitive fields enter logs, events or exports. Use bounded metric labels rather than raw user or prompt values, and keep authoritative audit records distinct from sampled telemetry. An absent trace may indicate sampling or propagation loss, not that no action happened.
Why: A provider span lacks its parent because context was not propagated into a worker. The dashboard shows two short traces rather than the real long request, so operators may misdiagnose latency until correlation is repaired.
Risk: High-cardinality labels can create excessive telemetry cost and expose identity.
Trade: Sampled traces aid diagnosis; durable audit state supports required accountability.
Try: Follow one request across a worker and verify safe identifiers without raw private content.
